title: Stones on Mount Ebal and Twelve Curses
summary: Moses and the elders command Israel, once across the Jordan, to set up large plastered stones on Mount Ebal, write the law on them, and build an altar of uncut stones for offerings. Six tribes are to stand on Mount Gerizim to bless and six on Mount Ebal for the curse, while the Levites pronounce twelve curses on secret sins, each answered by the whole people with Amen.
story: With the law code complete (chapters 12-26), Deuteronomy turns to the covenant ceremony that will seal it. Chapters 27 and 28 set out blessings and curses, the standard sanctions of an ancient covenant. Chapter 27 is a set of instructions for a ceremony to be held after the crossing, in the heart of the land at Shechem, between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim. The people are to write the law on stone, worship, and publicly accept the curses that will fall on those who break it. The ceremony is carried out in Joshua 8:30-35, after the fall of Jericho and Ai. The chapter's declaration that this day you have become the people of the LORD your God marks Israel's identity as settled before a single field of Canaan has been sown.
historical:
Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim stand on either side of a narrow valley in the central hill country, with the ancient city of Shechem (near modern Nablus) at the pass between them. Shechem was where God first promised the land to Abraham (Genesis 12:6-7) and where Jacob bought land and set up an altar (Genesis 33:18-20), so the ceremony returns Israel to the place of the first promise. Joshua later renewed the covenant there as well (Joshua 24).

The text raises two debated questions. First, the Samaritan Pentateuch, the version of the five books preserved by the Samaritan community, reads Mount Gerizim instead of Mount Ebal in verse 4, and the Samaritans built their temple on Gerizim. Most scholars think the Samaritan reading reflects their later claims, but some argue it may preserve an older text. Second, in the 1980s the Israeli archaeologist Adam Zertal excavated a stone structure on Mount Ebal from the early Iron Age (around the twelfth century BC) and identified it as an altar, possibly connected with this tradition. Other archaeologists have interpreted it as a watchtower or a farmstead, and the question remains open.
cultural:
Writing on plastered stone was a known practice. The stones were coated with lime plaster, and the text was written or painted on the smooth surface; an inscription in ink on plaster was found at Deir Alla in the Jordan valley, for example. Large monuments with public inscriptions were a way for ancient kings to proclaim their deeds and laws. Here the monument proclaims not a king's achievements but God's instruction, set up at the entrance to the land.

The altar of uncut stones follows the law of Exodus 20:25, which forbade shaping altar stones with tools, perhaps to avoid imitating the elaborate altars of other peoples or to keep human workmanship from claiming credit in worship. The curse ceremony relied on public speech: the Levites proclaim, and the people answer. Saying Amen meant accepting the terms, calling down the curse on oneself if one broke them. The twelve curses mostly concern acts done in secret, beyond the reach of any human court, such as private idolatry, moving a boundary stone at night, misleading a blind man, or murder unseen.
literary: The chapter has three parts, each introduced by Moses speaking with others: with the elders (verses 1-8), with the Levitical priests (verses 9-10), and alone (verses 11-26). The first part is framed by the instruction to write all the words of this law (verses 3 and 8). The curses form a list of twelve, perhaps one for each tribe, each with an identical structure: a curse formula, a description of the act, and the people's response. The list moves from sins against God (idolatry) to sins against parents, neighbors, the vulnerable, sexual order, and life, and ends with a summary curse on anyone who does not practice the law, which gathers the whole list into one.

outline.t: Plastered stones with the law and an altar on Mount Ebal
Today you have become the people of the LORD
Six tribes on Gerizim, six on Ebal

doctrines.note: The covenant is sealed with public words and public assent. Israel is the people of the LORD by his choice, and it accepts the obligations of that relationship with a corporate Amen.
The curses focus on sins committed in secret, where no court could reach. God sees what is hidden, and the covenant holds each person accountable before him even when no human witness exists.
The law is written on stone at the entrance to the land, publicly and distinctly. God's word is not a secret for priests but a public text for the whole people.

words.note: Arar, to curse. A curse was a solemn declaration that someone was cut off from God's favor and under his judgment. The passive participle cursed appears twelve times, and the repetition makes the chapter's weight felt. The first curse in the Bible falls on the serpent and the ground in Genesis 3.

Amen, surely or so be it. The word comes from a root meaning firm or reliable. By saying Amen, the people bound themselves to the terms. The word passed into Christian worship through the New Testament, where Jesus uses it to introduce his own solemn statements, usually translated truly.

Mizbeach, altar, literally a place of slaughter or sacrifice. The altar on Mount Ebal was to be built of uncut stones, and it was a place for burnt offerings and peace offerings. The ceremony joins law, sacrifice, and rejoicing in God's presence.

Gerizim, the mountain of blessing. It faces Mount Ebal across the valley at Shechem. The Samaritans later regarded it as the true place of worship, and the Samaritan woman raises the question with Jesus (John 4:20).

christ: Paul quotes the final curse in his argument that no one is justified by the works of the law: all who rely on the law are under a curse, because the law pronounces a curse on everyone who does not continue in all that is written (Galatians 3:10, citing verse 26). He then says that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), drawing on Deuteronomy 21:23. The chapter's list of curses shows how deep the law's demand reaches, into secret acts and the heart, and Paul reads it as showing the need for a redemption the law itself could not provide. The mountain setting also returns in John 4, where a Samaritan woman at the foot of Gerizim asks Jesus where true worship belongs, and he answers that the hour is coming when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth (John 4:20-24).

hard.q: Why does Moses write only curses here, and where are the blessings from Mount Gerizim?
hard.a:
Verses 12-13 set six tribes on each mountain, one group to bless and the other for the curse, but verses 15-26 record only curses. Readers have long noticed this. Some think the blessings are supplied by chapter 28:1-14, which follows immediately, and that chapter 27 records only the Levites' part of the ceremony. Others think the twelve curses were a separate liturgy of self-examination, distinct from the blessing-and-curse ceremony between the mountains. The account in Joshua 8:33-34 says that Joshua read all the words of the law, the blessing and the curse.

The emphasis on curses fits the chapter's purpose. These are sins that human courts could not punish, so the people submit themselves to God's judgment directly. The imbalance also anticipates the sober tone of chapters 28 to 30, which foresee Israel's failure and exile. The chapter doesn't deny the blessing; it makes plain that the covenant has teeth.

questions: Most of the curses fall on sins done in secret. What would change if you lived as though your hidden life were as visible as your public one?
The people answered each curse with Amen, accepting responsibility together. What does it mean to be accountable as a community and not only as an individual?
The law was written on stones at the entrance to the land. Where is God's word visibly placed in your home, your habits, or your community?
